interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
`user.greet()` prints **"Hi, Sam"**; `greetFn()` prints **"Hi, undefined"** (or throws in strict mode reading `this.name`) — same function, two different results, because `this` is decided by the call site, not the function's definition.

Walking each call:

- **`user.greet()`** — implicit binding. The object to the left of the dot, `user`, becomes `this` inside `greet`, so `this.name` is `"Sam"`.
- **`greetFn()`** — `greetFn` is just a reference to the same function value, now called bare with no object attached. That's the default-binding rule: `this` is `undefined` in strict mode (or the global object in sloppy mode), so `this.name` is `undefined`.

The underlying idea: assigning `const greetFn = user.greet` copies the **function value**, not a bond to `user`. Nothing about `greet`'s own definition remembers `user` — that link only existed at the moment of the `obj.method()` call shape, and it's gone the instant you extract the function as a bare reference. This is the exact same mechanism behind the classic "passing a method as a callback loses `this`" bug.

**Testing:** whether you can trace `this` per call site instead of assuming it's tied to the object a method was declared on.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Why do arrow functions behave differently from regular functions with respect to `this`, and when should you deliberately choose one over the other?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Arrow functions don't have a `this` binding of their own — they don't participate in the default/implicit/explicit/`new` rules at all. Instead, `this` inside an arrow function is resolved exactly like any other free variable: by looking outward through the **lexical scope chain** to the nearest enclosing non-arrow function, and using whatever `this` was there.

That single difference drives the choice:

- **Use a regular function** when you want `this` to depend on *how* the function gets called — object methods that are always invoked as `obj.method()`, prototype methods, anything meant to be shared and re-bound (`call`/`apply`/`bind` need a real `this` slot to act on).
- **Use an arrow function** when you want `this` to stay whatever it was in the surrounding code, regardless of how the arrow gets invoked — inline callbacks inside a method (`array.forEach(item => ...)`), event handlers defined as class fields, and any nested helper that should "just see" the outer `this` without a `bind` dance.

A concrete rule of thumb I use: if the function is a **method that gets called through an object**, make it a regular function or a class method; if it's a **callback passed somewhere else** and you want the surrounding `this`, make it an arrow. Mixing them up is the source of both the "lost `this`" bug and its opposite — accidentally rebinding an arrow's `this` when you meant it to track a specific object.

**Testing:** whether you understand the mechanism (lexical vs dynamic resolution) well enough to make a deliberate choice, not just "arrows fix `this` issues" as a slogan.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Design rationale

interviewQuestions.question: You're converting a React class component's event handler to make sure it always has the right `this` when passed to a child as a prop. What are your options, and what would you actually pick?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The bug being fixed is always the same shape: `<Child onClick={this.handleClick} />` extracts `handleClick` as a bare function reference, so when the child eventually calls it, it's an unbound call and `this` inside `handleClick` is `undefined`.

Three real options:

- **Bind in the constructor:** `this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this);`. Runs once per instance at construction, cheap, and keeps `handleClick` as a normal prototype-shaped method for anything else that wants to call it directly.
- **Class field arrow function:** `handleClick = () => { ... }`. No constructor boilerplate, and it's the pattern most teams default to now — but every instance gets its own function object instead of sharing one off the prototype, which matters if you're rendering thousands of instances.
- **Bind inline at render:** `onClick={() => this.handleClick()}` or `onClick={this.handleClick.bind(this)}` written directly in JSX. Simplest to read, but it allocates a **new** function on every render, which breaks `React.memo`/`shouldComponentUpdate` reference-equality checks on the child and can cause unnecessary re-renders.

My actual pick: the constructor bind for anything performance-sensitive with many instances, the class-field arrow for everything else since it reads cleanest, and I explicitly avoid the inline-bind pattern for props passed to a memoized child, since the reference-equality break is a real, measurable regression, not a style nitpick.

**Testing:** whether you can connect a `this`-binding mechanism to a concrete framework performance trade-off, not just recite the three fixes.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
`p` is **`undefined`** — `Person` has no `return` statement, so calling it like a normal function returns nothing. But `window.name` becomes **`"Alex"`**, silently.

The mechanism: without `new`, this is a bare call, so the default-binding rule applies. In sloppy mode (no `"use strict"`), default binding sets `this` to the **global object** — `window` in a browser — instead of `undefined`. So `this.name = name` inside the constructor-shaped function actually executes as `window.name = "Alex"`, quietly creating or overwriting a global property, while the caller gets back `undefined` and likely assumes the call simply failed.

Why it's dangerous in practice: there's no error, no warning — the bug surfaces later as some unrelated global (`window.name`, `window.id`, whatever the constructor happens to assign) mysteriously holding the wrong value, often far away from where `Person(...)` was mistakenly called without `new`.

Two real defenses: **strict mode** (`"use strict"` or ES modules, which are strict by default) turns the silent global write into `this` being `undefined`, so `this.name = name` throws immediately at the actual mistake instead of corrupting global state. And a guard inside the function — `if (!(this instanceof Person)) return new Person(name);` — makes the constructor safe to call either way, which is the pattern most pre-ES6 libraries used before `class` made a bare call to a class constructor a hard `TypeError` instead.

**Testing:** whether you understand default binding's sloppy-mode global-object fallback as a real production hazard, not just a `this === undefined` factoid.
